page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Pair the first two terms
steps.margin_note: First mark. Pair sin50° with sin70° using the sine DIFFERENCE formula, sinC − sinD = 2 cos((C+D)/2) sin((C−D)/2). Note the half-difference comes out NEGATIVE, and that is what makes it cancel.
steps.memory_tip: Pair sin50° with −sin70°. The half-difference comes out NEGATIVE, which is what makes it cancel.

recall.must_convey: That the first two terms are paired, giving 2 cos60° sin(−10°).
accept: pair the first two with the sine formula to get two cos sixty sin minus ten
combine sin fifty minus sin seventy into a product
the half difference is minus ten degrees
modati rendu ni combine cheste two cos sixty sin minus ten vasthundi
apply the sine difference formula to the first pair

steps.why: Pairing the two 50s and 70s leaves an angle of 10°, which is exactly the third term — that match is why the expression vanishes.

steps.label: Evaluate and cancel
steps.margin_note: Second mark. cos60° is 1/2, so the 2 cancels; and sin(−10°) is −sin10°, which cancels the third term exactly.
steps.memory_tip: cos60° = 1/2 cancels the 2, and sin(−10°) = −sin10° cancels the third term exactly.

recall.must_convey: That cos60° = 1/2 cancels the 2, and sin(−10°) = −sin10° cancels the remaining term to give 0.

steps.why: sin is an odd function, so sin(−θ) = −sin θ. That sign is what makes the last two terms annihilate rather than double.
common_mistakes: Writing sin(−10°) = sin 10° and getting 2 sin 10°.

insider_note: Pair sin50° − sin70° with the difference formula; the half-difference is NEGATIVE, giving sin(−10°). That minus sign is exactly what cancels the third term.
